newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street stocks seen opening higher.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street stocks seen opening higher.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to move higher at the start of trading Friday, as bonds got a boost from comments made yesterday by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan.

Greenspan said Thursday that he expected U.S. economic growth to decelerate later this year and into next, comments interpreted by some to mean that the Fed would not raise rates at the next FOMC meeting on May 20.
But even if it were to raise rates, a further tightening by 25 basis points has been discounted by the market.

"So far it looks like we will have a positive opening. I think we'll have an upward bias, but you never know once the programs kick in," said Hildegard Zagosrki, analyst at Prudential Securities. "The market is so volatile."
"A rate hike on May 20 is built into the market. But no one expects another hike after that. The feeling on Wall Street is that after May 20 that's it."
The stocks market will also be following through on a firm if volatile session yesterday which saw the Dow industrials close steadily firmer, but well off highs for the day.

Tokyo stocks ended lower in the Friday session, closing below the 20,000 threshold for the first time this week. Brokers said profit-taking by both foreign and domestic institutional investors hit the major indices as the yen strengthened against the dollar.
The 225-share Nikkei average fell 259.03 points or 1.29 percent to 19,802.78.
In London, the FTSE 100 was up 36.2 at 4616.6.
Most U.S. stocks were marked higher in London on Friday, tracking solid gains in the bond market.

Drawing the most investor interest in London was McDonald's Corp stock, quoted $3/8 lower at $53-7/8, after the Wall Street Journal reported that the fast-food giant's sales had fallen by some six percent since its discount hamburger promotion.
The dollar extended its losses against the yen in Tokyo on Friday due to fears of rises in Japanese interest rates but came off its lows by late trade.
The dollar was off its lows in Europe after dipping below 120 yen and 1.70 marks.
U.S. Treasuries were higher with the long bond up 17/32 to yield 6.89 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that Australian mall magnate Frank Lowy is attempting to raise as much as $460 million through a U.S. initial public offering of Westfield America. But several veteran REIT experts have turned thumbs down on the offering, for which Merrill Lynch is lead manager.
The New York Times Market Place writes that mutual fund investors, unfazed by April's stock market volatility, added some $13.5 billion to equity funds last month.
